title: Tracing platform
brief: Store distributed traces for 500 teams and make an exemplar link open the useful trace during an incident. Decide what to sample before storage, handle late spans, and keep query traffic from overwhelming ingestion. Keeping all errors is a policy goal with a failure boundary, not a magic property of sampling.

clarify.a: About 10,000 traces/s, 20 spans/trace and 500 bytes/span before compression. If average span residence is 30 seconds, budget about 3 GB of raw payload before overhead and redundancy. A 30-second decision timer alone does not establish residence time; span arrival patterns and decision caches also matter (approx.).

No. Plan a representative 10% baseline and prioritize error and slow traces subject to a hard byte budget. The modeled storage load is the 10% baseline. An error-heavy incident can exceed it, so reserve capacity or explicitly shed lower-priority samples.

Route a trace id to one decision group, persist decisions for a bounded late-span window and append late spans consistently where possible. Mark incomplete traces. Collector loss or upstream sampling can still remove evidence.

Retained 100 MB blocks and small trace-id reads after sampling. Tail assembly, outcome selection and full attribute searches are worked obligations; placing the Traces observer does not implement a tracing platform.

notes: Collectors see 10,000 traces/s with 20 spans/trace and 500 B/span. Retain 10% for seven days; a raw tail buffer holds spans for an assumed average of 30 seconds before selection (approx.).
One catalog batch is a 100 MB retained block. Raw collection and the selected-block workload have separate capacity boundaries.

The reference starts with already selected and formed blocks. The API acknowledges only after object storage accepts them durably. Raw-span collection, sampling, durable collector spooling and index publication need separate capacity and failure tests.
Sources emit only their assigned request types. The source rates below reproduce the aggregate workload; protocol guarantees still require the separate design checkpoint.

Scored data retention: at least 7 days on active authoritative stores. Copies used only for search or reports can be rebuilt. Local device history and rollup policies still require the separate protocol check.

text.name: Synchronized rush
text.description: Many callers send requests together instead of spreading them over time.

debrief.headline: A synchronized rush hit {node}.
debrief.fix: Spread scheduled work over time and keep spare capacity on the affected path. A rate limiter protects downstream work by rejecting excess calls, so it cannot by itself meet every availability target.

numbers.label: Illustrative raw tail buffer
numbers.how: 100 MB/s × assumed 30-second average residence, before metadata and redundancy (approx.).

hints: Does the sampling decision need to know whether the request eventually failed?
Head sampling saves network earlier but cannot see future errors. Tail sampling receives and buffers spans before choosing. Keep all spans of a trace on one decision group.
A sampler must expose lost evidence and preserve ingestion isolation under pressure. Measure the failed boundary, waiting time and retry work before choosing a change.

editorial.summary: Applications and collectors propagate trace context and redact sensitive attributes. Tail selection groups spans by trace id with a bounded decision window, a late-span policy and explicit overflow. The reference starts after selection and block formation: the API durably uploads blocks, then publishes trace-id lookup metadata. It measures neither raw collection nor the sampling guarantee. Tempo also supports attribute queries over columnar Parquet blocks; a trace-id lookup structure is not a description of all its search capabilities.

designs.name: Durable blocks with cached trace lookups
designs.why: The shared API durably uploads already selected immutable blocks and publishes lookup metadata idempotently. A crash after upload leaves an orphan that reconciliation can index. Cached object and index reads serve trace-id lookups; recent-query visibility requires a publication watermark. There is no 100 MB standard queue message. Real-time span reception and recent trace assembly sit before this scored boundary.

tradeoffs: Head sampling can discard the trace before an error occurs. Select consistently by trace id so services do not independently retain fragments.

Tail selection receives the raw stream before choosing. At an assumed 30-second average residence, this example buffers about 3 GB raw payload; arrival timing, process overhead, replicas, decision caches and long traces change that estimate.
At 100 MB/s raw, a hard 10 MB/s storage budget cannot keep every trace if errors dominate. Reserve capacity and prioritize, or declare a loss policy. Monitor dropped and incomplete traces.

A trace-id lookup path is cheaper than indexing every attribute. Attribute queries can use columnar block scans and selective indexes with a separate scanned-byte budget. Current Tempo supports TraceQL over Parquet; it is not limited to trace-id retrieval.

Keep complete request metrics for SLI denominators. Outcome-biased retained traces cannot directly measure the population error rate. Exemplars link selected observations without making trace ids metric labels.
editorial.realWorld: This example has about 200,000 spans/s before sampling. Ten percent baseline storage is about 864 GB/day before compression; actual retention rises when error-priority traces exceed the baseline. Collector buffering and query scans need separate measurements (approx.).

correctness.prompt: A collector has seen only successful spans when its tail decision timer expires. A late error span arrives afterwards. What is your policy and how is its loss measured?
correctness.discussion: Keep a bounded decision cache keyed by tenant and trace id so late spans follow an explicit prior decision or a documented promotion rule. Mark incompleteness, count late and dropped spans, and bound memory and decision lifetime. A head sampler upstream may already have removed evidence. Collector restart needs durable spooling and replay if the loss budget demands it. No tail policy guarantees all errors across unobserved or discarded spans. Request metrics must count the whole population independently. Tail sampling trades bounded waiting and memory for better whole-trace evidence. A decision deadline creates a failure boundary; late evidence may arrive after state was discarded. A sampler must expose lost evidence and preserve ingestion isolation under pressure.

fields.label: Step 1. A trace arrives with no error yet. May tail sampling decide immediately?
options: Drop immediately because the first span succeeded
Buffer until a declared decision deadline within memory limits
fields.explanation: Tail sampling trades bounded waiting and memory for better whole-trace evidence.

fields.label: Step 2. An error span arrives after its trace was dropped. Can keep-all-errors be guaranteed?
options: Yes, because the sampler always retains errors it sees in time
No; use an explicit late-span policy and measure missed error traces
fields.explanation: A decision deadline creates a failure boundary; late evidence may arrive after state was discarded.

fields.label: Step 3. A noisy tenant fills the sampling buffer during an incident. What protects others?
options: Per-tenant budgets, explicit overflow policy and sampling-loss metrics
fields.explanation: A sampler must expose lost evidence and preserve ingestion isolation under pressure.

correctness.limits: The traffic model does not execute this protocol. The checked trace covers its central responsibility; the written explanation is retained for review.
correctness.responsibility: Make tail sampling decisions within a bounded buffer and explain late-span loss.
